extracted.intended_audience: labor-law practitioners, employers, unions, agency decisionmakers, and policymakers evaluating or litigating joint-employer status under the NLRA
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation of when one entity is a 'joint employer' of another's employees under the NLRA, focusing on common-law agency principles, the list of essential terms and conditions, and the policy and procedural consequences of adopting particular tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise-of-control requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A putative joint employer must be shown to have exercised substantial direct and immediate control over the essential terms and conditions of another entity's employees; mere potential or reserved authority is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal appellate courts repeatedly focus on the extent to which a putative joint employer has exercised control. The dissent emphasizes proof that the putative joint employer `exercise[d] significant control' and that the common-law test looks to entities that `actually exercise control' over employees' essential terms and conditions. Cases cited: Felder v. U.S. Tennis Assn., Faush v. Tuesday Morning, Butler v. Drive Automotive, Whitaker v. Milwaukee County, Gulino v. N.Y. State Educ. Dept., Browning-Ferris Industries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserved contractual rights / indirect control insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: A contractual reservation of authority that is never exercised, and `indirect control' (conduct other than actually determining essential terms), standing alone does not establish joint-employer status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not a single circuit has held that an entity can be a joint employer based solely on a never-exercised contractual reservation or on indirect control. The dissent stresses that the standard promulgated by the majority wrongly dispenses with any exercise-of-control requirement and that the common law demands exercise of control rather than mere reservation or indirect influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common-law agency principles control NLRA test
rubrics_metrics.description: The NLRA requires application of common-law agency principles when determining joint-employer status; agency regulation must be grounded in the agency's judgment and consistent with statutory/common-law limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dissent repeatedly asserts that the Taft-Hartley Act and precedent make the common law of agency the controlling standard and that an agency must not adopt a regulation that exceeds common-law boundaries. Citations include Community for Creative Non-Violence v. Reid and administrative-law principles (Transitional Hospitals v. Shalala; Prill v. NLRB). The dissent finds the majority's standard inconsistent with common-law agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traditional list of essential terms and conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Essential employment terms relevant to joint-employer analysis include paying salaries, hiring and firing, and control over daily activities — broadly: hiring, supervising/directing, setting wages/benefits/hours, disciplining/discharging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts and precedent identify factors such as whether the putative joint employer `paid [the employees'] salaries, hired and fired them, and had control over their daily activities.' The dissent endorses a demanding standard focused on entities that `play a significant, active role in hiring, supervising, or directing another employer's employees, in setting their wages, benefits, or hours of work, and/or in disciplining or discharging them.' The 2020 Rule reflected this exercise-of-control approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction from the FLSA economic-reality test
rubrics_metrics.description: The NLRA joint-employer standard should not mirror the Fair Labor Standards Act's broader `economic reality' test that counts indirect control and total employment situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dissent distinguishes the NLRA/common-law test from the FLSA, noting that FLSA `economic reality' examines total employment situation and indirect control, which is `uniqueness of the FLSA.' The majority's new standard resembles the FLSA approach and is therefore inconsistent with common-law agency as applied under the NLRA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newly adopted essential term: work rules and directions (manner/means/methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: The majority added `work rules and directions governing the manner, means, or methods of work performance' as an essential term whose reserved or exercised control can indicate joint-employer status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dissent critiques this expansion as lowering the bar for joint-employer findings because many contracting parties reserve or require compliance with brand, quality, or safety standards that govern methods without creating an employer relationship. The majority declined to categorically exclude brand-protecting controls from relevance, leaving uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newly adopted essential term: working conditions related to safety and health
rubrics_metrics.description: The majority made `working conditions related to the safety and health of employees' an essential term of employment such that control or reserved authority over these matters may support joint-employer status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dissent argues this change is unsupported by common-law agency and unwise as policy. It notes OSHA's regulatory scheme and multi-employer doctrines (creating/exposing/correcting/controlling employers) and cites cases (Universal Construction Co. v. OSHRC; Knitter v. Corvias) showing that exercising or requiring safety measures does not traditionally create joint-employer status. The dissent warns that making safety/health an essential term will sweep in many entities simply complying with law or protecting premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence standard requires actual exercise rather than hypothetical or potential control
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board should require evidence that the putative joint employer would have exerted significant control (i.e., actually exercised it), not merely that it had the contractual ability to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Felder, dismissal was proper because plaintiff failed to allege that the putative joint employer `would have exerted significant control' had it not rejected a subcontractor's referral. The dissent uses this to argue that hypothetical or unexercised authority should not suffice to impose bargaining duties or other consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of real-world collective-bargaining consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulemakers must consider whether a joint-employer rule will facilitate or frustrate collective bargaining — e.g., whether adding additional parties at the bargaining table will make agreements less likely and create procedural chaos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dissent emphasizes that making entities that never exercised control into joint employers can `inject chaos' into collective bargaining (conflicting interests, impasse/implementation uncertainties). It asks practical questions about seating an entity that never exercised reserved authority at the bargaining table and the implications for bargaining, impasse, and implementation, concluding the final rule likely frustrates, not promotes, productive collective bargaining. Citations: NLRB v. Insurance Agents' Int'l Union; H.J. Heinz Co.; Auciello Iron Works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to meaningfully respond to public comments under the APA
rubrics_metrics.description: In rulemaking, the agency must engage with and respond to substantive public comments, including industry-specific and policy-based criticisms, and cannot dismiss them as legally irrelevant if its invocation of common-law constraints is incorrect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dissent faults the majority for `briefly describ[ing], but proceed[ing] to disregard' many comments about the rule's impacts (training, safety initiatives, DEI programs, contracting with small businesses, staffing, healthcare). The dissent states the Board has failed its statutory duty under the Administrative Procedure Act to provide a reasoned response to these comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of small-business and jurisdictional impacts (combining revenues)
rubrics_metrics.description: A broader joint-employer definition will bring more small businesses within the Board's discretionary jurisdiction by allowing combination of gross revenues of joint employers, increasing legal and bargaining costs for small entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dissent warns that lowering the joint-employer threshold will sweep greater numbers of small businesses (previously below jurisdictional thresholds) into NLRB oversight, saddling them with costs (e.g., attorneys for bargaining) and potential economic hardship, with little countervailing benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of neutral employers under Section 8(b)(4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expanding joint-employer status to entities that exercise indirect or reserved authority risks converting neutral employers into primary employers subject to picketing and boycotts, undermining Section 8(b)(4)'s protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dissent cites Section 8(b)(4) purpose to `shield[ ] unoffending employers' and warns the final rule's breadth will subject heretofore neutral employers to lawful picketing, especially where the joint employer has no real control over the contested essential term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects on successorship and rescuing moribund businesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Joint-employer findings should not create automatic bridging of bargaining duties that deter potential buyers from rescuing failing businesses by saddling successors with predecessor terms and conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dissent explains that if user businesses are deemed joint employers of a supplier's employees, they may be joint employers of the successor's employees, preventing a successor from setting initial terms different from the predecessor and discouraging acquisitions. It discusses Supreme Court precedent (Burns International Security Services; Fall River) and NLRB decisions (Whitewood Maintenance) about successorship and the public policy of facilitating business rescues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry-specific considerations — construction contractors and multi-employer worksites
rubrics_metrics.description: In industries like construction, where multi-employer worksites and coordination by general contractors are routine, ordinary supervisory or safety coordination should not automatically create joint-employer status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dissent highlights standard-form contract provisions (discipline, safety, supervision/coordination of means/methods) and argues the final rule risks finding general contractors joint employers of all subcontractors' employees despite Denver Building Trades precedent that `some supervision' does not eliminate independent-contractor/employer status. The dissent urges consistency with Denver Building & Construction Trades Council.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry-specific considerations — franchising and brand controls
rubrics_metrics.description: Controls franchisors reserve to protect brand standards (cleanliness, hygiene, operations) typically should not be treated as indicia of a common-law employment relationship; rule should clarify or exempt brand-protecting controls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters warned that the final rule's vague treatment of brand-protecting controls could make franchisors joint employers of franchisees' employees or force franchisors either to exert more control (turning owners into managers) or withdraw guidance (forcing franchisees to seek costly HR/legal help). The majority declined to categorically exempt brand-protection controls, leaving practical uncertainty and potential disproportionate impact on minority-owned businesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry-specific considerations — staffing firms and travel nurses (healthcare)
rubrics_metrics.description: Client reservation or exercise of authority over schedules, work rules, or safety practices at a host site can be treated as indicia of joint-employer status under the final rule, threatening staffing firms and healthcare staffing practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dissent notes staffing firms place temporary employees with clients; under the final rule virtually every client may be a joint employer because clients reserve or exercise authority over hours, scheduling, tenure, and work rules. For hospitals, maintaining work rules or health-and-safety policies on premises could render them joint employers of travel nurses, with significant administrative and patient-care consequences. Commenters warned about chilling effects on contracting with staffing firms and on ability to address staffing shortages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interplay with OSHA multi-employer doctrines and regulatory duties
rubrics_metrics.description: An employer's legal obligations under OSHA (including implementing safety standards for all employees on a site) and categorization under OSHA guidance (creating/exposing/correcting/controlling employer) should not, by themselves, be treated as creating joint-employer status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dissent observes OSHA requires employers to implement safety standards for all employees at a workplace and that OSHA guidance contemplates different types of multi-employer duties without converting those entities into joint employers. Case law (Universal Construction Co. v. OSHRC; Knitter v. Corvias) supports the proposition that applying safety measures for liability or statutory reasons does not create a common-law employment relationship; the dissent argues the final rule's treatment of safety/health control conflicts with this understanding.
